query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of HCP titanium (Ti) to the single-phase BCC NbMoTaW alloy will improve its room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance while preserving its BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW with poor room-temperature ductility
generation.intervention: Alloying with 5 at.% HCP titanium (Ti) through arc melting and subsequent annealing at 1200 °C for 24 hours
generation.conditions: Temperature range: up to 1600 °C; Helium implantation at energies between 10-100 keV
generation.structural_mediator: Introduction of HCP titanium (Ti) into the BCC lattice, potentially creating lattice distortions and enhancing atomic diffusion
generation.mechanism: The added Ti atoms will occupy substitutional sites in the BCC lattice, introducing local lattice distortions that enhance atomic diffusion and promote self-healing behavior under irradiation, thereby improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance
generation.predicted_outcome: 20% increase in room-temperature ductility (measured by tensile elongation) and 30% reduction in irradiation-induced hardness increase (measured by nanoindentation) compared to untreated NbMoTaW
generation.boundary: Temperature: up to 1600 °C; Helium implantation fluence: up to 1 × 10^17 ions/cm²
generation.uncertainty: The actual effect of Ti addition on the alloy's microstructure and properties may vary depending on the specific processing conditions and the resulting distribution of Ti atoms in the lattice

falsification_experiment.design: Tensile testing and helium implantation experiments on Ti-alloyed and unalloyed NbMoTaW samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-alloyed NbMoTaW sample exhibits less than 10% increase in room-temperature ductility or less than 20% reduction in irradiation-induced hardness increase compared to the unalloyed sample, the hypothesis is falsified
